argentina.note: Public-health administration competes with personal access; court safeguards remain relevant. Roadblock protocols are not proof of a general limited-area personal-search law. Incitement regulation is narrower than banning institutional criticism.

australia.note: Public-health access conditions, court-based preventive orders, designated weapons-search areas and racial-vilification restrictions coexist with constitutional freedoms. Vaccination permission is an outbreak-specific inference, not a claim of a current universal passport.

bangladesh.note: Health administration and security controls support qualified restrictions; restored court oversight qualifies prevention. Speech-law reform after 2024 does not remove all incitement regulation.

bhutan.note: Public-health responsibilities, judicial preventive safeguards and regulated public order favour qualified powers. Religious and social-harmony constraints supply contextual incitement evidence, not an exact modern statutory finding.

brazil.note: Public-health authority and judicial procedure support bounded prevention; abusive police practice conflicts with constitutional search limits. Racial-crime restrictions differ from general suppression of dissent.

canada.note: Public-health access conditions and judicial peace-bond powers are compatible with Charter safeguards. Canadian individual-search thresholds oppose broadly suspicionless areas. Hate-propaganda law reaches beyond direct violent threats with defined defences.

china.note: Health and security controls support permission; actual courts and censorship are not independent safeguards or equal protection of all groups. Qualified answers recognise the revised limits rather than treating every control as unlimited.

costa-rica.note: Health and judicial prevention coexist with strong personal-search protections. Broad expression rights compete with anti-discrimination obligations on the nonviolent incitement scenario.

cuba.note: Health and public-order administration favour permission. The reviewed-court wording receives qualified support because actual political remedies are constrained. Speech supervision does not establish equal application to every group.

denmark.note: Public-health restrictions, reviewable prevention, limited weapons-search zones and anti-incitement rules are bounded control mechanisms within a free constitutional system.

egypt.note: Health/security policing and speech restrictions support qualified permission. Actual court independence and selective protected groups remain substantial qualifications, so formal procedures are not freshly certified.

ethiopia.note: Health and conflict-related security administration favour bounded powers in principle. Uneven remedies, territorial implementation and selective speech enforcement qualify the exact responses.

france.note: Health-pass precedent, reviewable administrative restrictions, defined security checks and racial/religious hate-incitement offences distinguish ordinary control from abolition of safeguards.

germany.note: Public-health measures, judicial Land prevention and hate-incitement law support qualified intervention; Land variation and grounds for danger qualify area searches.

hungary.note: Public-health and security obligations coexist with judicial rights and speech restrictions. The exact group-neutral application and effective review remain qualified by institutional concerns.

india.note: Public-health administration and security prevention support qualified powers. Court review exists alongside delayed remedies; selective communal speech enforcement is not equal protection of every group.

indonesia.note: Health-access precedent and security/public-order regulation favour qualified controls. Current judicial corrections and selective religious-expression rules remain counter-evidence to unrestricted permission.

iran.note: Public-health and security administration favour controls, but judicial independence and universal group protection are not established by moral censorship. Qualified responses distinguish this bounded scenario from actual harsher coercion.

israel.note: Health-access and preventive security precedents support controls with important territorial differences. Civilian courts and occupied-territory practice differ; incitement rules are not merely direct threats.

italy.note: Health-access precedent, reviewed preventive measures and public-order search exceptions support bounded powers. Racial/religious incitement restrictions are distinct from all offensive speech.

japan.note: Voluntary vaccination/access concerns compete with public protection. Judicial prevention is compatible with rights; routine search thresholds remain individual. Hate-speech measures include noncriminal and local approaches, making general prohibition mixed.

malaysia.note: Health-access and security powers support qualified permission. Court oversight, religious-selective speech limits and their actual application qualify the four exact scenarios.

mexico.note: Public-health restrictions compete with limited universal vaccine-access rules. Preventive security has court roles; coercive policing conflicts with formal personal-search protections. Incitement regulation remains a qualified contextual estimate.

netherlands.note: Health-pass alternatives weaken a specifically vaccination-only condition. Reviewed exclusion orders, limited weapons-search areas and group-incitement law support qualified control without unrestricted police powers.

new-zealand.note: Health-access precedent and court-issued control orders support bounded intervention. Ordinary search requirements oppose broad area searches; racial hostility rules are narrower than general dissent suppression.

nigeria.note: Health and security administration favour qualified controls. Effective remedies and religiously selective enforcement remain uncertain; censorship alone is not proof of equal anti-incitement protection.

north-korea.note: Public-health access and warrantless policing favour control. A serious-violence finding with regular judicial review conflicts with political arbitrary prevention, so the reviewed scenario is mixed rather than assumed strongly supported. Incitement suppression is selective, not universal protection.

norway.note: Voluntary vaccination competes with outbreak-access protection. Reviewed prevention and limited police powers support qualified intervention; strong hate-incitement restrictions are distinguished from institutional criticism.

pakistan.note: Health and security institutions favour bounded controls. Actual judicial access and religiously selective speech regulation qualify precise responses; formal courts do not certify independent protection.

philippines.note: Health-access and strong policing favour qualified powers. Formal courts coexist with coercive practice; expression safeguards and intimidation conflict on general nonviolent group-incitement prohibition.

poland.note: Specific vaccination access is mixed across health administration and limited general pass rules. Judicial prevention receives support; exact area-search authority is less established than ordinary policing. Group-incitement law supports qualified restriction.

russia.note: Health/security obligations and broad policing favour control. Court form and selective extremism enforcement qualify rather than establish the new review and group-protection requirements.

saudi-arabia.note: Health-access and security supervision favour controls. Court and speech applications are selective; the exact independently reviewed and group-neutral interpretation is not treated as documented.

singapore.note: Health-access conditions and racial/religious harmony laws favour bounded control. Internal Security Act detention does not itself demonstrate judicially reviewed prevention; qualified rather than strong support preserves that distinction.

south-africa.note: Public-health duties compete with bodily autonomy on vaccine access. Judicial remedies, authorised area searches and hate-expression constraints differ from arbitrary general intrusion.

south-korea.note: Past health passes compete with limits on mandatory vaccination; judicial prevention fits procedural safeguards. Individual search requirements and limited general hate-speech legislation qualify the two other mechanisms.

spain.note: Public-health access precedents, reviewable prevention, public-security search powers and group-incitement restrictions support bounded authority with legal qualifications.

sweden.note: Voluntary vaccination and public-health access compete. Reviewed exclusion powers, security zones and agitation-against-group offences support qualified controls despite strong general expression rights.

switzerland.note: Health certificates can permit alternatives to vaccination. Contestable prevention, cantonal search powers and anti-discrimination speech rules favour qualified control; cantonal variation remains disclosed.

taiwan.note: Vaccination promotion and access autonomy compete. Court-supervised prevention fits recent safeguards. Risk-location policing is narrower than blanket area searches; broad expression rights and anti-discrimination duties compete on nonviolent incitement.

thailand.note: Health/security administration and strong speech controls favour qualified permission. Political-content laws do not by themselves prove neutral racial/religious protection or effective regular review.

turkey.note: Health-access and security administration support controls. Judicial and selective speech-enforcement concerns qualify the precise conditions rather than supplying unlimited agreement.

ukraine.note: Public-health and wartime safety powers favour qualified permissions. Wartime urgency and court access remain scope qualifications; restrictions on incitement are not a universal peacetime speech ban.

united-arab-emirates.note: Health-access and security powers favour qualified control; preventive judicial review and selective group-expression enforcement remain limits of the retained evidence.

united-kingdom.note: Vaccination-only access competes with alternative certificates and rescinded sector mandates. Reviewed preventive orders, time-limited authorised searches and racial/religious stirring-up offences support bounded controls with different statutory thresholds.

united-states.note: Federal/state vaccine-access differences are substantively mixed. Courts can impose risk-based preventive restrictions; suspicionless area searches conflict with Fourth Amendment individual grounds outside narrow exceptions. Nonviolent hateful expression remains strongly protected rather than equated with direct threats.

vietnam.note: Health and security administration favour qualified restrictions. Political suppression is broader than the new reviewed-court or protected-group mechanisms and does not establish impartial enforcement.

alt-lite.note: Anti-censorship and anti-mandate commitments compete with strong law-and-order preferences; court review and credible danger make prevention more compatible than arbitrary intrusion.

american-conservatism.note: Communicable-disease protection competes with medical choice across the constitutional strand. Court-limited prevention and threat-grounded policing coexist with arms and nonviolent-expression protections.

anarcho-capitalism.note: Self-ownership and rejection of state monopoly coercion oppose all four state permissions; private rights-based responses to aggression are not the government powers in these statements.

authoritarian-capitalism.note: Security administration and managed expression favour qualified permissions. Predictable procedures can matter, but regular meaningful judicial limits are not automatically its central commitment.

christian-accelerationism.note: The specified escape-from-coercion and strong national-order strands compete on medical and expressive control. Security prevention has stronger fit; faith alone does not supply vaccine or hatred policy.

christian-conservatism.note: Protection of neighbours competes with bodily conscience; orderly policing supports bounded prevention. Religious protection competes with concern that nonviolent incitement bans can restrict doctrine and expression.

christian-democracy.note: Human dignity and common-good duties justify proportional collective-safety measures with review, while subsidiarity and expression rights constrain their scope.

christian-social-democracy.note: Social responsibility favours collective health and protection from group hostility; dignity and personal-search rights qualify suspicionless area powers.

christian-socialism.note: Collective responsibility and protection from domination favour bounded health and incitement measures. Civic organising and personal-search safeguards qualify policing without individual suspicion.

civic-nationalism.note: Equal civic membership supports outbreak protection and restrictions on group-hostility incitement. Common civic duties do not automatically justify every suspicionless search.

classical-liberalism.note: Harm prevention can justify reviewed restraint of serious threats. Communicable externalities compete with personal choice on access; broad nonviolent expression and individual search grounds oppose the other permissions.

communism.note: The retained party-state scope favours health and security control. Judicial limits and equal group protection are qualified by actual doctrine rather than assumed from later state labels.

communitarianism.note: Responsive communal obligations permit bounded shared-safety and anti-hostility measures with privacy and remedies retained. The common good does not mean unchecked executive coercion.

conservative-centrism.note: The One Nation/ECHR scope accepts proportional health, security and hate-incitement rules while maintaining judicial review and wider speech protections.

constitutional-monarchism.note: Constitutional safeguards accommodate reviewed prevention. Monarchy itself settles neither vaccine access nor incitement bans; autonomy and proportional public obligations substantively compete in the retained scope.

cuban-socialism.note: Health and security administration support qualified state permissions. Meaningful review and equal speech protection are not freshly established by formal civil-rights language.

cultural-nationalism.note: Cultural self-development and autonomous expression compete with communal protection. Reviewed serious-harm prevention is compatible; the exact modern health and area-search prescriptions remain conditional.

democratic-socialism.note: Collective public health and protection from targeted hostility coexist with abolitionist policing and bodily freedom; court safeguards do not eliminate all preventive-control objections.

ecosocialism.note: Collective harm prevention and anti-domination support health and group-protection measures while civil organising and search safeguards oppose wider policing of nonsuspects.

environmentalism.note: Public-health protection is compatible with civil liberties. Protest freedoms and individual grounds qualify area searches; group-incitement restrictions remain narrower than general dissent bans.

fascism.note: Strong state discipline favours health and policing control; independent regular review conflicts with sovereign coercion. Selected-group protection competes with its own exclusionary mobilisation, so broad incitement prohibition is mixed.

green-politics.note: Shared health and protection of minorities coexist with participatory civil rights and scepticism of coercive policing; prevention and personal autonomy remain conditional.

hindu-nationalism.note: National safety and social discipline favour bounded powers. Protection of religious groups is selective and competes with mobilisation against other groups, preventing a uniformly strong incitement-ban inference.

islamic-fundamentalism.note: Common moral/security duties favour control. Protection of religious community competes with oppositional mobilisation and limits on plural toleration; private faith is not evidence of every policy.

islamic-socialism.note: Collective welfare and public order support bounded health, security and group-protection permissions, with actual historical coercion and civic participation supplying counter-evidence.

islamism.note: The specified political-religious state scope permits health and expression supervision. Selective toleration and judicial practice qualify rather than establish equal protection and independent review.

kantian-republicanism.note: Rightful general law can prevent injury under review; autonomy and external protection compete on vaccination access. Arbitrary personal searches and nonviolent thought/expression bans have weaker fit.

left-wing-populism.note: Pluralist organising and collective protection favour health and anti-incitement measures; dissent and individual search safeguards qualify policing nonsuspects.

liberal-conservatism.note: Personal choice and lawful order support reviewed prevention and credible-threat policing. Communicable health and nonviolent incitement generate genuine autonomy/public-protection tension.

liberal-feminism.note: Protection against harm and group hostility coexist with bodily autonomy and equal basic liberties. Suspicionless policing raises competing personal-security concerns.

liberalism.note: The retained international liberal rights framework allows proportional harm prevention; free expression competes with nonviolent group-protection regulation, and individual-search thresholds remain stronger.

libertarianism.note: Medical choice and free expression oppose broad state conditions and nonviolent censorship. Protective courts can restrain credible serious threats; that does not confer suspicionless area policing.

luxemburgism.note: Self-emancipation and open political discussion oppose bureaucratic control; collective defence and shared health compete with liberty on the exact modern preventive scenarios.

maoism.note: Collective mobilisation favours health/security control; meaningful regular review and neutral protection against hostility conflict with the enemy/people distinction.

marxism.note: The retained emancipatory theory combines collective harm prevention with opposition to political policing and censorship. Transitional coercion and autonomous organising create substantive conflicts on these modern mechanisms.

meritocracy.note: Public competence and equal opportunity support health and reviewed protection; inquiry and impartial personal treatment compete with nonviolent incitement and nonsuspect searches.

militarism.note: Civilian-institutional security priorities favour shared-safety controls, with strong threat-grounded policing. Civilian review and lawful public discussion still qualify the doctrine.

minarchism.note: The minimal protective state can stop objectively credible rights violations under courts, but personal medical choice, individual search grounds and nonviolent expression constrain its powers.

nationalist-conservatism.note: Common duties and policing coexist with personal freedom; vaccine and group-incitement restrictions are conditional in this constitutional-order variant.

nazism.note: Racial mobilisation and selective protection conflict with broad nonviolent group-incitement prohibition. Meaningful judicial review also conflicts with security terror; broad police and population control otherwise remain central.

neoconservatism.note: Security prevention has strong fit with retained constitutional safeguards. Collective health and group protection compete with individual and speech liberties rather than following foreign-policy force.

neoliberalism.note: Individual choice and predictable law accommodate reviewed prevention; medical externalities, privacy and expression create conditional exact-policy applications. Market scores do not supply these answers.

nordic-social-democracy.note: Collective safety and protection from group hostility coexist with independent legal remedies and expression. The concrete retained Nordic institutional strand accepts bounded controls.

objectivism.note: Objective protection against credible force can justify reviewed prevention. Nonviolent expression and individual grounds remain protected; shared infection risks qualify medical choice without abandoning autonomy.

postmodernism.note: The specified critique of disciplinary power opposes preventive and nonsuspect policing; care for vulnerable groups and resistance to coercive normalisation compete on medical access and speech regulation.

progressive-liberalism.note: The Deweyan public-responsibility strand accepts collective safety and protection from group hostility; inquiry and personal safeguards qualify suspicionless search.

republicanism.note: Non-domination permits contestable collective protection. General incitement rules and suspicionless searches must be reconciled with non-arbitrary expression and personal-security safeguards.

right-wing-populism.note: The retained Reform programme opposes medical coercion and broad speech controls while strongly favouring credible-threat policing and preventive security with courts.

social-anarchism.note: Voluntary solidarity can protect against disease and hostility, but state access conditions and police coercion conflict with the anti-hierarchy doctrine. Opposition to the mechanism is not approval of harm.

social-democracy.note: Collective health and protection from group hostility coexist with rights against arbitrary detention and search. Individual-search safeguards qualify security-area powers.

social-liberalism.note: Effective freedom and proportionate prevention of harm support health and group-protection regulation; individual search rights remain a substantive limit.

socialism.note: The retained democratic/anti-domination school supports shared health and protection from hostility while civic autonomy constrains nonsuspect policing. Later authoritarian practice is not substituted.

thatcherism.note: Law-and-order and counterterrorism controls coexist with medical choice, parliamentary safeguards and expressive freedoms in the retained historical programme.

third-way.note: Active public protection combines health, crime-prevention and group-incitement rules with legal safeguards and civil inclusion.

traditional-conservatism.note: Ordered liberty supports reviewed prevention and credible-threat policing, while bodily conscience and nonviolent expression compete with communal obligations.

trotskyism.note: Anti-bureaucratic mobilisation and collective defence generate genuine tensions on modern health/preventive mechanisms; open political discussion opposes broad nonviolent censorship.

zionism.note: The specified historical civic-security doctrine supports reviewed protection; health, search and group-expression scenarios remain conditional rather than imported from a contemporary government.

abraham-lincoln.note: Wartime collective obligations support health/security analogies; habeas suspension conflicts with regular remedies. Constitutional expression competes with restrictions on dissent and group hostility.

adam-smith.note: Natural liberty and predictable justice accommodate preventing credible injury; shared infection protection competes with medical access autonomy. Nonviolent expression receives stronger protection than broad censorship.

adolf-hitler.note: Population discipline and police power favour control. Meaningful regular review conflicts with terror; racial mobilisation conflicts with protecting groups from nonviolent hatred even as favoured-group expression is controlled.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.note: Public-health protection and resistance to targeted group hostility coexist with strong immigrant privacy and limits on preventive/suspicionless policing.

andy-burnham.note: Public protection and health duties support bounded measures; Hillsborough accountability particularly requires meaningful review. Wider speech protections remain alongside incitement restrictions.

angela-merkel.note: Public-health and security intervention, regulated expression and proportional legal remedies coexist. The vaccination-only access scenario is a qualified inference rather than a universal German rule.

angus-taylor.note: Individual choice and free expression constrain medical and speech permissions; documented intelligence/criminal enforcement favours reviewed prevention and credible-threat policing.

anthony-albanese.note: His pandemic public-protection coordination and pursuit of stronger incitement restrictions favour bounded authority, alongside civil rights and courts. The 2025 proposal is his preference rather than proof every proposed offence passed; precise vaccination access and state search powers remain inferred.

augusto-pinochet.note: Security and population discipline favour intervention, but meaningful regular review conflicts with political coercion. Selective protection and censorship compete on a general group-incitement ban.

ayn-rand.note: Objective rights allow protection from credible force with courts. Medical coercion, searches of nonsuspects and nonviolent speech restrictions have weaker fit; infection risks qualify bodily choice.

barack-obama.note: Public-health and counterterrorism responsibilities favour bounded protections; constitutional nonviolent expression competes with opposition to harmful group hostility.

benito-mussolini.note: State discipline favours health and policing controls. Independent review conflicts with coercion; exclusionary mobilisation competes with selective protection against hostile expression.

benjamin-netanyahu.note: Health-pass and preventive security precedents support qualified controls, with civilian judicial rights and occupied-territory differences retained. Incitement restrictions are not only direct violent threats.

bernie-sanders.note: Public-health duties coexist with strong due-process and search protections. Anti-hostility commitments compete with constitutional protection of nonviolent expression.

bill-gates.note: Vaccination and responsible shared-health institutions favour bounded access protection; civil safeguards and expression compete with nonsuspect search and hate-incitement bans. No philanthropic role establishes a personal police platform.

bob-hawke.note: Public-health responsibilities, racial discrimination safeguards and ordinary policing favour bounded measures while independent civil institutions constrain scope. Historical vaccination access remains an analogy.

boris-johnson.note: Pandemic certification and personal-liberty objections compete on vaccination-only access. Security/public-order and British incitement rules coexist with legal remedies.

charles-de-gaulle.note: Collective wartime protection and policing favour controls; constitutional freedom competes with exceptional speech restraint on the nonviolent incitement scenario.

clement-attlee.note: Public-health and emergency administration support bounded obligations; civic expression and public-order intervention compete on nonviolent group-incitement prohibition.

deng-xiaoping.note: Security and public administration support control, but regular meaningful review conflicts with suppression. Qualified incitement permission is not proof of equal protection for all communities.

donald-trump.note: Explicit opposition to COVID vaccine mandates weighs against access conditions while security enforcement supports bounded prevention/searches. Constitutional speech rhetoric and selective suppression of targeted groups create a genuinely mixed incitement response.

dwight-d-eisenhower.note: Collective health and Cold War protection favour bounded obligations; constitutional expression competes with loyalty/security speech constraints.

edmund-burke.note: Ordered liberty permits serious-harm prevention under law. Personal conscience and communal obligations compete on medical and nonviolent group-expression controls.

elon-musk.note: Medical choice and explicit broad free-expression commitments oppose coercive access and nonviolent censorship. Prevention of credible violence is compatible with courts; area policing competes with individual autonomy.

emmanuel-macron.note: Health access and security regulation, including incitement controls, coexist with contestable legal measures and wider civil freedoms.

fidel-castro.note: Public-health and security discipline favour control; independent regular review is in tension with political coercion. Selective speech controls do not establish equal group protection.

franklin-d-roosevelt.note: Wartime collective protection supports health/security measures; internment conflicts with regular remedies, and civil-rights language competes with dissent restrictions.

frederick-douglass.note: Equal security and constitutional remedies favour reviewed prevention. Medical autonomy competes with collective health; free expression and opposition to discriminatory policing constrain broader permissions.

friedrich-hayek.note: General law can prevent injury while protecting a private sphere. Communicable externalities compete with medical choice; nonsuspect searches and nonviolent censorship have weaker fit.

george-w-bush.note: Public-health and counterterrorism responsibilities favour bounded measures; constitutional speech protections compete with security-driven restraint on group hostility.

george-washington.note: Lawful civil protection supports reviewed prevention; private choice, historical communal obligations and constitutional expression create mixed modern medical and incitement applications.

gough-whitlam.note: Health provision, legal aid and racial equality favour collective safeguards and incitement restraint, while stronger personal rights qualify suspicionless area policing.

harry-s-truman.note: Collective health and Cold War security support bounded control; vetoes of restrictive anti-subversion measures qualify interference with nonviolent expression.

hillary-clinton.note: Public-health/security administration favours safeguards with enforcement; opposition to harmful hostility competes with constitutional nonviolent speech protection.

ho-chi-minh.note: Collective health and wartime security favour permissions; independent regular remedies fit poorly with party discipline. Speech control is selective rather than universally protective.

hugo-chavez.note: Public welfare and security favour intervention. Weakened remedies qualify reviewed prevention; selective incitement control is not equal freedom for dissenting groups.

indira-gandhi.note: Population-health and security intervention favour control; emergency suspension of safeguards conflicts with regular independent review. Qualified speech restriction is distinct from uniform group protection.

jacinda-ardern.note: Pandemic access conditions and public protection coexist with courts and free criticism. Group-incitement regulation is a qualified programme inference rather than assuming every proposed reform passed.

javier-milei.note: Personal freedom and voluntary choice oppose medical/speech coercion; strict enforcement against disruption makes credible-threat policing more compatible than arbitrary control.

jawaharlal-nehru.note: Collective public health and preventive security coexist with constitutional rights; speech restrictions concerning communal hostility support qualified permission.

jd-vance.note: Explicit anti-mandate and anti-censorship commitments coexist with border/criminal security priorities. Munich criticism of nonviolent speech enforcement supports opposition to incitement prohibition; courts and credible danger distinguish these policing scenarios.

jean-jacques-rousseau.note: Common civic obligations favour shared health and public-order regulation. The connection between civic liberty and discipline qualifies exact modern safeguards and expression restrictions.

jeff-bezos.note: Explicit personal-liberty commitments permit warrants and credible-threat intervention; collective health competes with choice, and nonsuspect searches compete with individual grounds.

jeremy-corbyn.note: Collective health and serious-harm prevention coexist with strong civil liberties; nonviolent expression and protection from group hostility compete, while intrusive area policing has weaker fit.

jimmy-carter.note: Public health and lawful safety support bounded measures; personal-search safeguards and expression rights compete with broader police and incitement restrictions.

joe-biden.note: Vaccination and public-safety administration support bounded obligations; constitutional expression competes with opposition to group hostility beyond direct threats.

joh-bjelke-petersen.note: Strong public-order and moral regulation favour bounded health, policing and expression controls, with formal civilian review retained as a qualification.

john-f-kennedy.note: Collective health and security protection favour bounded intervention; civil-rights and speech commitments compete with anti-subversion restraints.

john-howard.note: Preventive anti-terrorism powers and public protection favour bounded controls; drug and gun restrictions do not alone supply health or incitement answers.

john-locke.note: Preservation under standing laws supports reviewed serious-harm prevention. Conscience, toleration and personal security compete with communal medical and speech obligations in the historical scope.

john-maynard-keynes.note: Public welfare and personal moral freedom coexist; reviewed protection fits while medical externalities, speech liberties and personal-search rights qualify other controls.

john-rawls.note: Equal basic liberties permit necessary collective protection under fair procedure. Nonviolent expression and equal security compete with incitement bans; individual grounds constrain wider searches.

john-stuart-mill.note: Preventing contagious injury and credible threats differs from coercing self-regarding welfare. The harm principle still protects nonviolent unpopular expression and constrains searches without individual grounds.

joseph-stalin.note: Population and security discipline favour control; regular meaningful judicial review conflicts with terror. Selective group-expression enforcement is not treated as universal protection.

julia-gillard.note: Public-health, anti-discrimination and security responsibilities favour bounded controls while civil institutions retain remedies.

justin-trudeau.note: Health-access and hate-propaganda restrictions coexist with Charter protections and personal freedoms; exceptional policing is not treated as unlimited discretion.

kamala-harris.note: Public-health and prosecution responsibilities favour bounded intervention; constitutional expression and protection from group hostility create a mixed nonviolent incitement response.

karl-marx.note: Collective protection competes with emancipation from bureaucracy on modern medical and preventive controls. Opposition to censorship gives stronger protection to nonviolent expression.

keir-starmer.note: Public health, stronger policing and British incitement laws coexist with rule-of-law commitments. Legal remedies remain a condition rather than evidence of unrestricted liberty.

kim-jong-un.note: Health and security control favour intervention; independently reviewed restraint conflicts with actual arbitrary prevention. Group-expression supervision is selective, not impartial protection.

lee-kuan-yew.note: Collective health and racial/religious harmony regulation favour control. Security detention weakens meaningful judicial review, so the safeguard-qualified prevention claim is mixed.

liz-truss.note: Personal choice and anti-censorship commitments constrain medical and expression regulation; public protection supports courts, while exact area policing competes with individual freedoms.

lula-da-silva.note: Public health and anti-discrimination commitments favour bounded measures; civic freedom and individual search safeguards qualify broader policing.

lyndon-b-johnson.note: Health and security administration coexist with civil-rights guarantees; nonviolent expression and group-hostility protection generate substantive tension.

mahatma-gandhi.note: Conscience and nonviolent resistance oppose coercive state mechanisms even where health and intercommunal peace are valued. Opposition to prohibition does not endorse hostility or infection.

mao-zedong.note: Collective discipline favours health/security control. Meaningful review and broad group-protection restrictions conflict with revolutionary enemy/people mobilisation.

marco-rubio.note: Public-health protection competes with opposition to blanket mandates, considered within his retained period. Strong security favours bounded court/police controls; constitutional nonviolent speech limits incitement prohibition.

margaret-thatcher.note: Law-and-order and counterterrorism commitments favour bounded controls. Medical choice and speech liberties compete with collective protection in these modern scenarios.

mark-zuckerberg.note: Recent medical-choice and reduced-censorship direction opposes broad access and expression controls. Credible threats and court safeguards permit narrower intervention; platform moderation is not a state prohibition.

martin-luther-king-jr.note: Protection of vulnerable people supports shared-health safeguards; coercive prevention and discriminatory policing remain serious concerns. Free speech and opposition to group hostility compete on general prohibition.

mary-wollstonecraft.note: Reasoned independence supports personal choice and expression while equal protection can justify reviewed prevention. Medical and police applications remain conditional historical inferences.

matt-canavan.note: Free expression and resistance to coercive medical requirements coexist with ordinary criminal enforcement; his opposition to broad hate-speech laws directly informs the incitement interpretation.

mikhail-bakunin.note: Anti-state coercion rejects reviewed state policing as well as arbitrary policing; voluntary mutual protection differs from compulsory health access and speech prohibition.

mikhail-gorbachev.note: Public-health/security administration persisted during liberalisation. Glasnost and inherited control create genuine tension on nonviolent incitement prohibition.

milton-friedman.note: Personal medical choice competes with communicable externalities; protective courts can prevent credible injury. Individual grounds and broad nonviolent expression constrain wider police and censorship powers.

nancy-pelosi.note: Public-health and security institutions receive support alongside oversight; constitutional nonviolent speech and protection from hostility generate a substantive mixed response.

narendra-modi.note: Health and security administration favour bounded powers; selective communal speech enforcement competes with broad protection of groups. Formal courts and actual restrictions are distinguished.

nelson-mandela.note: The rights settlement permits proportionate collective protection while protecting expression and remedies. Anti-hostility safeguards are narrower than dissent suppression; personal searches remain conditional.

nigel-farage.note: Anti-mandate/free-expression commitments coexist with strong police and security priorities, giving different responses to medical, speech and credible-threat mechanisms.

paul-keating.note: Public health, security administration and racial-vilification rules favour bounded authority; courts and broad civil rights remain meaningful constraints.

pauline-hanson.note: Explicit opposition to vaccine mandates and hate-speech restrictions coexist with tougher criminal enforcement. Public-order preference does not erase medical or expressive liberty positions.

peter-thiel.note: Voluntary choice and expressive freedom coexist with enthusiasm for security infrastructure. Credible-threat measures have stronger fit than medical coercion or general nonviolent censorship.

recep-tayyip-erdogan.note: Public-health and broad security authority favour controls; actual court independence and selective speech enforcement qualify each precise bounded mechanism.

richard-nixon.note: Public-health and law-and-order institutions favour intervention; constitutional expression competes with coercive security and political restraint.

rishi-sunak.note: Vaccine-access restrictions compete with reversals and narrower public-health rules. Strong policing and British incitement regulation support bounded authority with judicial constraints.

robert-f-kennedy.note: Collective health and organised-crime protection favour bounded measures; civil-rights and constitutional expression compete on general nonviolent incitement prohibition.

robert-menzies.note: Public-health and anti-communist order responsibilities favour bounded controls, with constitutional courts and selective religious/racial context qualifying modern analogies.

ronald-reagan.note: Vigorous lawful enforcement supports reviewed prevention and credible-threat policing. Collective health competes with personal medical choice; constitutional expression weighs against prohibiting nonviolent incitement as such. Arms rights remain independently sourced.

rosa-luxemburg.note: Self-emancipation and open discussion oppose bureaucratic policing; collective defence and shared health compete with autonomy on the precise modern access/prevention mechanisms.

ruhollah-khomeini.note: Collective health and moral/security control favour permission; independent regular review conflicts with revolutionary coercion and speech protection remains religiously selective.

rupert-lowe.note: Explicit medical, expression and self-defence liberties coexist with strong law enforcement. Courts and a credible danger distinguish bounded policing from personal-choice restrictions.

salvador-allende.note: Public health and civil pluralism favour collective safeguards; free organising and personal security qualify suspicionless area policing. Incitement restraint remains narrower than dissent prohibition.

scott-morrison.note: Pandemic and national-security coordination favour bounded protections while legal remedies remain. Federal/state responsibilities qualify attributing every exact access/search rule personally.

theodore-roosevelt.note: Public protection and vigorous enforcement favour bounded measures; civic criticism and regulatory order compete on nonviolent group-incitement prohibition.

theresa-may.note: Public-health safety and medical choice compete; preventive security, policing and British incitement rules support qualified authority with legal review.

thomas-hobbes.note: Sovereign protection favours health and speech supervision; meaningful independent regular challenge conflicts with the sovereign model, despite self-preservation rights.

thomas-jefferson.note: Limited government and civil liberty compete with historical collective protection on modern medical and police scenarios; nonviolent expression has stronger protection.

tony-abbott.note: Shared-health and counterterrorism obligations favour bounded intervention; opposition to broad speech regulation competes with protection against religious/racial hostility.

tony-blair.note: Public protection, reviewed control orders and racial/religious hatred regulation favour bounded authority alongside Human Rights Act freedoms. Identity registration is not reintroduced as compulsory carrying.

vladimir-lenin.note: Collective health and revolutionary security favour control; independent regular review and broad group-protection rules conflict with suppression and revolutionary mobilisation.

vladimir-putin.note: Health/security control favours permissions; meaningful independent review conflicts with actual political restrictions. Speech enforcement is selective rather than equal community protection.

volodymyr-zelenskyy.note: Public-health and wartime security favour bounded safeguards with important urgency/territorial qualifications; hate-incitement regulation is not a general peacetime dissent ban.

winston-churchill.note: Collective health and wartime protection favour controls; peacetime civil liberties and exceptional restraints compete on nonviolent group-incitement prohibition.

xi-jinping.note: Health and security administration favour state permission; independent regular review conflicts with party control and group-expression regulation is selective.

zohran-mamdani.note: Collective health and opposition to hate incidents coexist with sanctuary privacy and limits on intrusive police searches. Anti-hostility protection is narrower than blanket political censorship.
